strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and computationally attractive: because mimic scores are computed only against a (possibly layer-specific) reference, per-sample gradient computation is cheap and requires no downstream datasets or auxiliary trained influence models, which distinguishes it from prior gradient-based selection methods (GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match).

The evaluation covers a sensible progression: a controlled label-noise simulation on six image datasets (where gains are substantial, e.g., average 68.60 vs. 53.33 for SGD under full fine-tuning), followed by realistic large-scale CLIP training on DataComp small/medium pools, spanning linear probing, full fine-tuning, and from-scratch pretraining.

The Stage 2 ensemble filter via weak supervision (Snorkel) is a clever reuse of an existing tool to aggregate noisy per-step assessments across training, and yields very high noise-detection F1 scores (often >95) in the controlled setting.

The dataset-quality estimation analyses (Pearson -0.903 with injected noise level; 0.958 with performance gain across filtered DataComp sets) and the novel 'predicting the pretraining dataset' experiment (Table 5) are interesting, original applications that go beyond simple accuracy claims.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: an explicit algorithm (Appendix B), layer names used in the reference CLIP, temperatures swept, hardware, and honest disclosure that broken DataComp URLs make results not directly comparable to the leaderboard.
weaknesses: A significant confound is not adequately addressed: in the CLIP experiments the reference model (CLIP-ViT-B-32-DataComp.XL-s13B-b90K) was trained on DataComp-1B, and Table 5 itself demonstrates that mimic scores partially recover the reference model's training set membership. This suggests mimic scores may partly encode overlap/memorization with the reference model's pretraining data rather than intrinsic sample utility, which could contaminate the DataComp results. The paper presents the membership-prediction result as a feature without discussing its implications as a confound.

The headline claim that mimic-score filters 'improve upon existing filtering methods' is only partially supported: in Table 4, the mimic-score-only filter underperforms the CLIP-score baseline (0.143 vs. 0.165 on Small scale), and gains over CLIP-score appear only when combined (0.163-0.164, i.e., slightly below the CLIP-score baseline on Small; only +0.002 on Medium). The improvement over the strong baseline is marginal and within what could be run-to-run variance, yet no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere.

Stage 1 gains on DataComp are small (0.131 -> 0.139 on Small; 0.254 -> 0.258 on Medium) and ImageNet/retrieval metrics are essentially unchanged; the broad framing around foundation models is not backed by any non-vision (e.g., LLM) evidence despite the introduction citing FineWeb/LLaMA/GPT-4.

The theoretical grounding is thin: the assumption that the straight-line direction from current weights to a reference model is a meaningful 'desirable' direction is justified only heuristically; nonconvexity, scale/architecture mismatch between the training model and reference, and the choice of which layer/weights to mimic (only text vs. image encoder last MLP layers are compared) receive little analysis.

In the full fine-tuning simulation, the reference model is trained on the noise-free version of the same dataset with a different seed — a favorable setup that does not test the realistic regime where the reference is trained on different or partially overlapping data; combined with the DataComp overlap concern, the strongest claims rest on somewhat circular setups.

Presentation issues reduce polish: several typos ('a more optima part', 'Peason correlation', 'encourages Grad-Mimic converges'), and unconventional 'Expected Results' subsections that state expectations rather than interpretation; the limitations discussion (Appendix A.1) is brief and does not engage the reference-data confound or the marginal CLIP-score gains.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem (sample-level data selection for foundation model training) and the core idea—scoring samples by the projection of their gradient onto the vector toward a pretrained reference model—is intuitive, simple to implement, and avoids needing downstream evaluation data.

The experimental program is reasonably broad: controlled label-noise simulations across six datasets (Table 1, Table 2) with strong detection F1 scores, CLIP training at two DataComp scales (Tables 3-4), dataset quality estimation correlated with noise level (Fig. 4a), and a creative 'predicting the pretraining dataset' analysis (Table 5).

The two-stage design (training-time reweighting plus cross-step aggregation of filter outputs via weak supervision) is a sensible way to mitigate noise in per-step gradient signals, and the algorithm is clearly described with an appendix pseudocode.

The paper is honest about some weaknesses, e.g., the footnote acknowledging broken DataComp URLs that limit leaderboard comparability, and the discussion that an unreliable reference model risks refining suboptimal datasets.
weaknesses: Circularity in the main large-scale experiment undermines the central claim. The reference model (CLIP-ViT-B-32 trained on DataComp-XL, 1.4B samples) was trained on data drawn from the same pool that the small/medium pools are subsampled from, so 'mimicking' toward the reference may largely amount to implicit distillation from a model trained on overlapping data rather than principled data selection. The 'predicting pretraining dataset' result (Table 5) directly reflects this overlap; only ~43% overlap still indicates the mechanism is mostly recovering samples seen by the reference model, not measuring intrinsic sample utility.

The headline claim that mimic scores 'improve upon existing filtering methods' (Abstract, Conclusion) is not supported by the paper's own tables. Mimic-score-only filters substantially underperform the CLIP-score baseline at both scales (0.135-0.143 vs. 0.165 small; 0.268 vs. 0.321 medium), and the complementary gains over CLIP Score are marginal (0.321 to 0.322-0.323), likely within run-to-run variance. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere.

Stage 1 gains are small and inconsistent: best-case improvement over standard training is ~0.013 (small) and ~0.004 (medium) average over 38 tasks. In the simulation experiments (Table 1), several results are anomalous and unexplained (e.g., Grad-Mimic's STL10 accuracy is non-monotonic in noise level: 72.06, 71.85, 83.09; Grad-Match's CIFAR10 collapses from 44.48 to 37.59 while Grad-Mimic jumps to 90.52), raising questions about run variance or evaluation issues.

The simulation setup embeds an optimistic assumption: the reference model is trained on the noise-free version of the same dataset (App. C.1). This does not validate the paper's claim that publicly available pretrained models can serve as references in realistic settings where the reference's training distribution differs; the DataComp experiment, which tests that claim, is exactly the one weakened by the overlap issue above.

No theoretical or empirical justification is given for why a straight-line projection in weight space onto (theta_ref - theta_t) should track sample utility; the argument implicitly assumes local linearity/convexity of the loss landscape, which is unmotivated for deep networks, and the choice to mimic only a last-layer MLP weight is ad hoc (image encoder works better than text encoder for reasons left unexplored).

Prior work on gradient-alignment-based selection (gradient matching, GraNd/EL2N, AGRA, influence functions, TracIn-style per-sample signal aggregation) is closely related; the delta over these is a different alignment target plus off-the-shelf Snorkel aggregation, which is a modest contribution.

Presentation and rigor issues: the normalized score in Eq. (2) reuses the symbol m for the unnormalized score, 'more optima part,' 'Peason correlation' (twice), 'Frequencxy' in Fig. 5, and a typo-laden reference style; Figure 1's caption claims 'Mimic scores closely align with their CLIP scores,' yet the paper's own Figure 6 reports a Pearson correlation of only 0.279—contradicting the framing. The per-sample-gradient cost at batch size 4096 for CLIP training is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the acknowledged broken URLs in DataComp mean the reported numbers cannot be directly compared to published DataComp results, weakening the external significance of the medium-scale gains.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and clearly presented: using the projection of a sample's gradient onto the direction toward a pretrained reference model's weights as a proxy for sample utility avoids the need for downstream datasets or separately trained influence models.

The paper is organized as a coherent framework (Mimic Score metric, gradient reweighting in Stage 1, and weak-supervision aggregation of per-step filters via Snorkel in Stage 2), and the connection to the weak-supervision literature is a nice and somewhat unusual combination.

Experiments cover two regimes: a controlled label-noise study on six image classification datasets and large-scale CLIP training on DataComp (10M and 100M samples), evaluated with the standard DataComp 38-task benchmark.

Useful auxiliary analyses: clear separation of mimic-score distributions for correct vs. mislabeled samples (Fig. 3), correlation between estimated dataset quality and noise levels (-0.903) and performance gains (0.958) (Fig. 4), and the novel 'predicting the pretraining dataset' experiment (Table 5).

Appendices provide the full algorithm, hyperparameters (temperatures, layer choices), compute details, and a temperature ablation; the authors also transparently note that broken DataComp URLs limit comparability to the leaderboard.
weaknesses: The central metric is largely heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding. There is no analysis of why the projection onto θref − θt (per-layer, last-layer only) is a reliable proxy for sample utility, how it relates to influence functions, or when the assumption ℓ(θref) < ℓ(θt) suffices. The direction toward a reference point in weight space need not correspond to a descent direction for the true objective.

Absolute gains at scale are modest and the metric is weaker than the strongest baseline as a standalone filter: in Table 4, Mimic Score Top-k filters (0.135/0.143 small; 0.268 medium) substantially underperform CLIP Score (0.165 small; 0.321 medium), and the only competitive results come from pruning the bottom scores on top of the CLIP-score filter (e.g., 0.323 vs 0.321). The paper's framing somewhat overstates this complementary result relative to the large gap to the primary baseline.

In the DataComp experiments, the reference model is trained on DataComp-1B, i.e., data drawn from the same pool being curated (and arguably closely related to the curated subsets). This in-domain reference raises a potential confound/circularity concern, especially for the 'predicting the pretraining dataset' experiment, and the paper does not test sensitivity to reference models trained on disjoint data.

In the simulation experiments the reference model is trained on the noise-free version of the same dataset, a favorable setup; robustness to imperfect or mismatched reference models—which the limitations section acknowledges qualitatively—is not empirically characterized.

Baseline implementations appear fragile: GraNd and AGRA collapse on several datasets in full fine-tuning (e.g., 0.62–2.78% on Flowers102), suggesting under-tuning rather than a fair comparison, and no error bars or seeds are reported anywhere, making small gains (e.g., 0.254→0.258) hard to interpret.

The computational overhead of per-sample gradient computation is not quantified. In fine-tuning the authors sidestep this by mimicking only the last layer, but the claim of 'computational feasibility' for training from scratch (where the full weight vector or chosen layers must be differentiated per sample) is not supported with wall-clock or memory comparisons.

Validation is limited to vision (supervised fine-tuning and CLIP); despite motivation via foundation models and web-crawled corpora more broadly (e.g., FineWeb/LLMs), no evidence is given for other modalities, and there is no clear guidance on how the approach transfers where no strong public reference model exists.

Presentation issues: odd section heading 'Expected Results' for actual results, repeated typos ('Peason correlation', 'more optima part'), and Figure 1's claim that mimic scores 'closely align' with CLIP scores sits awkwardly with the reported per-sample correlation of only 0.279 in Figure 6.

strengths: The core idea is simple, practical, and well-motivated: score samples by projecting their negative gradient onto the vector toward a pretrained reference model's weights, avoiding the need for curated validation sets, extra forward passes, or influence-function machinery.

Empirical evaluation is broad and fairly thorough: controlled label-noise experiments across six image datasets and two fine-tuning regimes (Table 1), large-scale CLIP pretraining on DataComp small/medium scales (Tables 3-4), comparisons against gradient-based baselines (GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match), Rho-Loss (Table 6), and approximated influence functions (Fig. 6), plus efficiency benchmarks (Fig. 7).

Useful ablations: temperature sensitivity (Table 9), choice of which layer to mimic (Table 10), and importantly the impact of reference-model quality via weight corruption and data-limited reference training (Fig. 9, Table 11), which addresses the most obvious objection to the method.

Interesting secondary applications are demonstrated convincingly: dataset-quality estimation via retention rate (Pearson -0.903), performance-gain prediction (0.958), and reverse-engineering a reference model's training set membership (Table 5, 42.6% overlap with DataComp'23 winner).

Honest treatment of limitations and potential bias propagation through the reference model (Appendix G), plus a companion ablation showing robustness to degraded references; theoretical analysis and full algorithms are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix A) is not fully convincing. Lemma A.2 claims (σ(v)-σ(0))ᵀ(v-0) ≥ (1/λ)‖σ(v)-σ(0)‖² 'since σ(·) is λ-Lipschitz', but Lipschitzness only bounds the norm of the difference; the stated lower bound on the inner product requires an alignment/monotonicity property that is not established. The one-step relative bound in Theorem A.4 also rests on restrictive conditions (small η, small κ, small ϵ) whose plausibility for real CLIP training is not verified, so the 'converges faster' claim is more intuition than proven result.

Absolute gains at scale are modest. At DataComp small scale the 38-task average improves from 0.131 to 0.146; at medium scale from 0.254 to 0.258 with ImageNet accuracy slightly worse (0.171→0.169). The mimic-score-only filter (top 30-40%) also underperforms the CLIP-score baseline (0.135-0.143 vs 0.165), and its value is mainly as a complement to remove low-scoring samples — the headline framing overstates the standalone filter's strength.

Novelty is moderate: the score is a heuristic projection closely related to excess-loss prioritization (Rho-Loss) and gradient-alignment selection; the positioning against these related methods could be sharpened, and the mechanism why mimicking last-layer weights of a differently trained (and for CLIP, possibly differently scaled) reference model generalizes is not deeply analyzed.

Some experimental settings are underspecified or confusing: which CLIP architecture is trained from scratch versus used as reference (the reference is ViT-B/32, implying the trained model must share parameter shapes), the note that DataComp URLs are broken makes leaderboard comparability uncertain, and in the fine-tuning experiments the claim of reweighting 'all model parameters' while only mimicking the last layer deserves clearer justification.
No code release is explicitly promised, which limits reproducibility given the many tuned components (temperature, binarization scheme, Snorkel aggregation, choice of mimic layer).
Writing has rough edges (e.g., 'Expected Results' subsections read like a proposal, several typos, inconsistent notation in Appendix A between v_t and the vector v in Lemma A.2).

strengths: The proposed Mimic Score is computationally simple: it reuses per-sample training gradients and requires no extra forward passes or curated validation sets, which is a genuinely practical advantage over Rho-Loss and influence-function approximations.

The experimental scope is broad and reasonably thorough: controlled label-noise experiments on six image datasets, comparisons against GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match, Rho-Loss and influence-function variants, CLIP training on DataComp small- and medium-scale pools, plus ablations on temperature, mimicked layer, and reference-model quality.

The weak-supervision aggregation (Snorkel) of per-step binarized scores is a sensible way to stabilize noisy single-step decisions, and the qualitative analyses (mimic-score distributions separating correct/incorrect labels in Fig. 3, caption-length patterns in Fig. 5, dataset-quality correlations) support the claim that the score is informative.
Limitations and potential misuse (biased reference models) are discussed in Appendix G, and the reference-quality degradation study (Appendix F) is a useful robustness analysis.
weaknesses: The headline large-scale gains are very small and statistically unsupported: on DataComp the average-over-38-tasks improvement is 0.131→0.146 (small scale) and only 0.254→0.258 (medium scale), with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests. A 0.004 gain at 100M scale could easily be run-to-run variance.

The mimic filter alone underperforms the CLIP-score baseline it claims to complement (e.g., 0.135 vs 0.165 on small scale; Mimic Top 30% is 0.268 vs Bearer [REDACTED] 0.267 at medium scale). Its main reported value comes from removing a small fraction of CLIP-score-selected samples, which is a much narrower contribution than the framing suggests.

The central assumption — that the vector θref − θt in weight space points toward a 'more optimal part of the weight space' — is unexamined. Why does a non-convex weight-space difference between two independently trained models define a meaningful descent direction? The claim that reweighting only last-layer gradients guides full fine-tuning of the entire model (Sec. 5.1) is asserted but never mechanistically explained.

The theoretical analysis (Appendix A) is weak and possibly flawed: Lemma A.2's invocation of softmax being 'λ-Lipschitz' to obtain f(λ)−f(0) ≥ (1/λ)‖σ(λ)−σ(0)‖² is not justified (the softmax Lipschitz constant does not scale that way, and the inequality direction is dubious), and the resulting Theorem A.4 is a one-step comparison under conditions (small η, small κ, small ϵ) that appear hard to verify in practice.

The method's claimed efficiency advantage over vanilla SGD is overstated: Fig. 7 shows ~0.67s per batch vs 0.031s for mini-batch SGD (~20x), and per-sample gradients at batch size 4096 for CLIP plus storing the n×T mimic-score matrix (e.g., 100M samples × T steps for the offline stage) raise nontrivial compute and storage costs that are not accounted for.

The authors acknowledge that some DataComp URLs are broken, so their results are not comparable to prior leaderboard numbers; combined with no released code being mentioned, reproducibility is limited.

Novelty is moderate: the score is essentially a fixed-target variant of gradient-alignment/impact metrics (e.g., Rho-Loss, AGRA) with the validation gradient replaced by a weight-space difference vector, and the DataComp gain relies on reusing existing strong filters.

Presentation has notable sloppiness (e.g., 'Peason correlation' in Fig. 4, awkward 'Expected Results' subsections, inconsistent notation between main text and appendix), which reduces confidence in overall polish.

strengths: The core idea—scoring sample utility by the projection of per-sample gradients onto the vector toward a reference model's weights—is simple, compute-efficient, and clearly distinguished from prior gradient-based selection methods that require noise-free validation sets or influence function machinery.

The two-stage framework (online reweighting plus offline aggregation of binarized scores via weak supervision/Snorkel) is a sensible packaging, and the ensemble filtering over training steps is a thoughtful way to reduce noise in single-step assessments.

Evaluation spans both controlled settings (six datasets with simulated label noise, two fine-tuning configurations) and realistic large-scale settings (CLIP training from scratch on DataComp small/medium scales, ~100M samples), with relevant baselines including GraNd, AGRA, Grad-Match, Rho-Loss, CLIP-score filtering, and approximated influence functions.

Extensive appendix analysis: efficiency benchmarks (runtime, GPU memory, convergence steps), ablations on temperature, layer choice, and degraded/weaker reference models, and a novel 'predicting pretraining dataset' analysis showing overlap with reference training sets.

The limitations discussion (Appendix G) is honest, including the risk of biased reference models, and the degradation experiments directly probe the method's dependence on reference quality rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix A) is weak relative to its billing. Lemma A.2's proof is not rigorous as written: the claimed inequality is asserted from a Lipschitz property where the stated bound (co-coercivity-type, with a 1/λ factor) does not follow directly from Lipschitzness, and the direction of the inequality needs a genuine monotonicity/co-coercivity argument. The main result (Theorem A.4) only establishes a one-step comparison under restrictive conditions (small η, small κ, θref near θ*), so it provides limited support for the headline claims about accelerated convergence.

Some headline claims are weaker than they first appear. The mimic-score filter alone substantially underperforms the CLIP-score baseline at the small scale (0.135 vs 0.165 average), and the main Stage-2 contribution is a modest complement to existing filters—removing 4.7M samples while performance stays roughly flat (0.322–0.323). The abstract framing ('training improved CLIP models with 4.7 million fewer samples') somewhat overstates a near-neutral performance change.

Mimic scores correlate strongly with CLIP scores (Pearson 0.279 on random samples, near-identical rankings in Fig. 1), raising the question of whether the method adds signal beyond a cheaper proxy for caption-image alignment; the paper does not fully disentangle this, e.g., no comparison of a CLIP-score-filter complement applied in the other direction or analysis on tasks where the two disagree.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance are reported for the main tables, and gains in Table 3 (e.g., 0.135 vs 0.131, 0.258 vs 0.254) are small enough that run-to-run variance matters. The footnote about broken DataComp URLs further complicates comparability with leaderboard results.

The simulation setup has mild circularity: the reference model is trained on the noise-free version of the same dataset, so the metric can exploit knowledge of the target distribution; although the appendix probes degraded references, the main results' strength may partly depend on this idealized reference availability.

Writing/presentation issues: 'Expected Results' subsections read like internal planning notes rather than paper prose; typos ('noise is naturally presented', 'Peason correlation'); and the theory-only-covers-GD limitation is not clearly connected to the SGD/Adam settings used in experiments.
